source.title: GeoLLM: Extracting Geospatial Knowledge from Large Language Models
source.authors: Rohin Manvi; Samar Khanna; Gengchen Mai; Marshall Burke; David B. Lobell; Stefano Ermon

record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream task performance across fine-tuned language models of different stated sizes, a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small pretraining runs, or optimize parameter-token allocation. Its relevant results are downstream task scores compared across models; the authors infer that performance scales with model and pretraining-data size.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes LMs of very different sizes (RoBERTa 125M, GPT-2 124M, Llama 2 7B, GPT-3.5) on the same geospatial tasks and reads the score ordering as scaling with model and data size. This is a weak, confounded downstream comparison, not a controlled sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main claim is that GeoLLM (prompts built from OpenStreetMap map data plus fine-tuning) extracts geospatial knowledge, beating baselines by 70%. The scaling statement is an inference from GPT-3.5 beating Llama 2 by 19% and RoBERTa by 51%. The authors cite Kaplan et al. but fit no law.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes language models for geospatial prediction and evaluates downstream-task scores; it does not reproduce pretraining runs or measure held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported downstream scores vary with task and number of fine-tuning samples. The paper also reports that prompt components affect task performance, but those ablations do not test scaling-law claims.
record.problems: Model comparison is not a controlled parameter-count sweep: GPT-3.5's parameter count is not stated, model families and fine-tuning procedures differ, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The scores are downstream geospatial metrics rather than pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's non-language-model baselines and the supplemental few-shot comparisons in Table 3 are omitted because they do not provide additional controlled evidence about performance scaling across the compared fine-tuned language models.

untested.parts: No power-law fits in other regimes.
Predictability is untested: there is no fitted relation, no loss-to-task mapping, and no controlled size sweep within one family.

missing.what: GPT-2 (124M) column of Table 1: a same-size counterpoint to RoBERTa, consistently lowest (e.g. 0.26/0.18/0.00 on WorldPop). It is a language model, so the 'non-LM baselines' exclusion doesn't cover it.
Mean r2 at 1,000 samples across tasks: GPT-3.5 0.68, Llama 2 0.57, RoBERTa 0.45.
10-shot GPT-4 beats 10-shot GPT-3.5 on all four tasks (e.g. Home Value 0.79 vs 0.55).

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak. Only a handful of models are compared, and they differ in family, objective (regression vs generation), fine-tuning method (full fine-tuning, 4-bit QLoRA, closed API) and pretraining data. GPT-3.5's size is undisclosed. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Predicting losses of larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares downstream scores across several model families, but does not fit a quantitative scaling relation, measure pretraining loss, or test whether scores can be predicted from scale.
Dependence of exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and bending of loss curves.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 vs Llama 2 7B vs RoBERTa-base, at 100 and 1,000 training samples
relationships.reason: Scores order by size in every task. Examples: WorldPop 100 is 0.61/0.43/0.00 (R07–R09); Home Value 1,000 is 0.87/0.74/0.50 (R52–R54).
relationships.display_finding: GPT-3.5, Llama 2 7B, and RoBERTa-base scored in descending order on every task, including WorldPop at 100 samples (0.61/0.43/0.00) and Home Value at 1,000 samples (0.87/0.74/0.50).

relationships.reason: Size gaps shrink to near zero: Women BMI ties at 0.63 (R28, R29), and Sanitation is 0.65/0.63/0.62 (R22–R24).
relationships.display_finding: Size gaps nearly disappeared, with Women BMI tied at 0.63 and Sanitation scores at 0.65/0.63/0.62.

relationships.condition: Models of equal size from different families (GPT-2 124M vs RoBERTa 125M), Table 1 text
relationships.reason: Based on the text, as no row records GPT-2. GPT-2 scores far below the same-size RoBERTa (WorldPop 10k: 0.26 vs 0.60), so family and fine-tuning method, not size alone, drive scores.
relationships.display_finding: GPT-2 124M scored 0.26 versus RoBERTa 125M's 0.60 on WorldPop with 10,000 examples, showing substantial differences at similar size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The three compared fine-tuned language models across the Table 1 tasks and training sample sizes
reader_labels.reason: Across the reported comparisons, GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 scores are generally above RoBERTa scores; the paper summarizes GPT-3.5 as outperforming Llama 2 and RoBERTa by 19% and 51%. This is downstream-score evidence, not a fitted prediction law (rows R01–R57).
